A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ActionStudio and contain readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Renamed models and reordered experiments can be matched. Appendices A.1–A.2 and Figures 2–5 are unchanged apart from pagination.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning results on NexusRaven and the CRM Agent Benchmark, a data-processing ablation, and measured training throughput.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and reports additional model and framework comparisons, an expanded preprocessing ablation, and a human audit of filtering decisions.

M1.justification: v3 introduces explicit rule-based trajectory filtering alongside critique filtering and an automatic training-profile router conditioned on model architecture, size, and available resources. The two-pipeline design, Unified Format 2.0, in-context and fine-tuned critics, and principal fine-tuning approaches already appear in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate NexusRaven and CRM and describe function-calling, tool-use, and robotic training data. v3 identifies ActionStudio-98k, its sources, and its 97,755 trajectories, whereas v1 describes an unnamed curated collection. The PDFs do not establish whether the represented training data changed or became more precisely documented.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds GPT-4.1-2025-04-14, Llama-4-Maverick-400b-inst, and Llama-4-Scout-109b-inst. AgentOhana enters both the CRM comparison and preprocessing ablation. The throughput comparison adds AgentOhana and Lumos, whereas v1 measured only ActionStudio. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated learning-rate ceiling from 2e-5 to 2e-4, without establishing that experiments were rerun. v3 specifies matched cluster/GPU controls for framework comparisons and a random, dataset-stratified audit of 150 trajectories. Existing benchmark sizes, metrics, and throughput configurations remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The existing CRM preprocessing ablation gains an AgentOhana-processed condition using the same corpus (v1 Table 3 to v3 Table 4). Human validation is expanded into a specified independent audit of filtering decisions. The scaling and long-context analyses were already present in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The newly specified audit sample concerns evaluation design; its changed agreement percentage does not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores, original ablation entries, and ActionStudio throughput values are retained. Added results include NexusRaven F1 scores of 0.843, 0.796, and 0.788 for GPT-4.1, Maverick, and Scout; AgentOhana CRM average accuracy of 0.80; and extensive framework throughput comparisons. v1's approximately 70% human-agreement statement is replaced by 85% in a specified audit, without establishing a same-setting improvement.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theoretical results or proofs. The appendix descriptions of the data schemas, tool-call parsing, and NexusRaven metric definitions are unchanged.

C1.justification: v3 adds a central claim of up to 9 times higher throughput than competing agentic frameworks, explicitly frames critique-and-filter as a novel contribution, and foregrounds the named ActionStudio-98k release with quantified scope. These extend v1's general claims of efficiency, curated data release, and benchmark effectiveness.

C2.justification: v3 discusses residual human disagreement and possible self-consistency checks, domain-specific detectors, and adaptive thresholds. It also attributes long-context efficiency to memory scheduling. Its new interpretation that AgentOhana trails on every ablation metric contradicts Table 4, where AgentOhana has higher free-text accuracy, 0.84 versus 0.82. Section 6's limitations remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds dataset provenance and composition, evaluation temperature zero, and a dated GPT-4o identifier. However, it removes substantial implementation documentation covering model loading, library choices, ZeRO stages, YAML-based dataset mixing, checkpointing/offloading, FlashAttention 2, and logging. The code-access URL and appendix implementation examples remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including TACO, AgentBank, PRACT, LAM Simulator, StableToolBench, and LoRA, while removing several implementation-related references. It emphasizes comparisons with AgentOhana and Lumos and strengthens the filtering novelty framing. The related-work sections retain their central argument about missing agent-specific infrastructure.

P1.justification: The abstract and contributions are substantially rewritten; data-pipeline descriptions become numbered subsections; and the detailed model/data/training-handler narrative is reorganized. Training efficiency and ablation sections exchange order and receive extensive rewrites. Experimental model names change from xLAM to ActionStudio, while the appendices remain unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn. The throughput table becomes a grouped framework comparison with colored percentage differences and support statuses; benchmark tables expand and move; and the ablation table is reordered and reformatted. Its new best-score highlighting incorrectly favors 0.82 over 0.84 for free-text accuracy. Appendix Figures 2–5 retain their displays.

improvement.justification: v3 supplies external framework comparisons on matched hardware, addressing v1's lack of comparative efficiency evidence, and strengthens validation through additional baselines and a documented human audit. These gains are tempered by substantial loss of implementation detail and incorrect ablation ranking and interpretation in Section 4.6/Table 4. The evidence supports a limited net improvement.
